RF Chain Budget

A receive or transmit chain stage by stage, each stage a System block with its own parameters - gain, noise figure, intercepts, compression, sensitivity and dynamic range in closed form, an N-way array included, or a transmitter's output power, back-off, ACLR and noise floor - and one action that writes the chain as test benches whose simulations put a number beside every one of them.

What it is

A chain budget is the spreadsheet every receiver and transmitter starts as: an ordered list of stages, each with a gain, a noise figure and an intercept, and the cascade worked out stage by stage. The RF Chain Budget is that table, with two differences that matter here:

  • Every stage is a part circuitRF already has. An amplifier stage is the System Amplifier with the Amplifier's own Gain, NF, IP3 and IP3Ref; a filter stage is the Filter with its own Response, Form, band and IL. The budget reads each part's numbers the way the part's model behaves.
  • One action turns the chain into a simulation. Transfer to Schematic writes the chain as test benches of those same parts, with the analyses that check the budget already set up and the budget's numbers written beside the simulated ones. The cascade is closed-form arithmetic; the check is circuitRF's own S-parameter, harmonic-balance and envelope analyses.

Opening it

  • Tools ▸ RF Chain Budget opens a new chain: an LNA, a filter and a second amplifier.
  • A .cchain in the workspace tree opens on a double-click.
  • File ▸ New ▸ Examples ▸ RF Chain Budget has a 2.45 GHz superhet, a four-element steered array, a front end with a canceller, a dual-conversion receiver, a 26 GHz link and a 3.5 GHz linear transmitter, each already transferred.

The window has three parts, and every edit recomputes all of them at once:

  • The chain, input on the left, drawn two ways that share one selection:

    • Blocks: one idealised block per stage, drawn with its System block's own symbol, with its own gain, NF and intercept under it and the cascade at its output (Σ) under that. An array is drawn compactly: the branch's stages once, each marked "× N", into one combiner block drawn as its variant — a direct combiner one N:1 symbol, a tree its levels of 2:1 (a deep one as "× levels"), an amplifier after each when it is active. A filter's block shows its band form. Drag a block left or right to move its stage: a line shows where it will land. Delete removes the selected block's stage. Right-click for Insert Block ▸ a part, which inserts a stage of that part where you clicked (the left half of a block before it, the right half after it), Copy, which puts the whole lineup on the clipboard as a picture to paste into a slide or a document, and Remove Block, which removes the block you clicked. Tick Levels for the level diagram under the blocks, a node on each gap.
    • Schematic: the schematic Transfer would write, drawn as every circuitRF schematic is, without the bench's sources, analyses and isolators: each stage is its own parts (a composed stage its composition, a tree its levels of Combiners), and in an array every element's branch is drawn into the combiner. Above each stage are four lines: its own gain and NF, its own intercept and compression point, and the cascade's gain, NF, IIP3 and SNR at its output. Scroll to zoom, drag with the middle button to pan. Z and a drag zoom to a box, and F, the Fit button or a double-click fits. Right-click ▸ Copy copies it as the schematic editor copies: a picture for a slide or a document, and parts and wires to paste into a schematic.

    Clicking a block, or a part in the schematic, selects its stage, and the selected stage is drawn selected in both. A click off every block or part, or Escape outside a text box, clears the selection.

  • The stages, one row each: the name, the part, and the part's parameters. Selecting a stage in either view scrolls its row to the top of the list.

  • The cascade, the levels and the canceller, Data Display tabs: the cascade table, one row per stage; the levels at every node, the budget's lines with the transferred benches' simulated points once they have run; the Link tab, with the link's and the receiver's inputs and numbers; a tab for each sweep the chain asks for; and, for a chain with a canceller, its depth against its errors. The chain's totals are below them.

Drag the gap between two of the three parts to give one more height.

Undo and Redo (the toolbar, or Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z, ⌘ on a Mac) step through every edit: an input, a stage's name, part or parameter, and every stage added, removed or moved. A value typed into a box is one step. Undoing back to the chain as it was opened or last saved leaves it unchanged, with nothing to save.

A value the budget cannot use is never taken. While you type one, its box is outlined in red, the reason is under the chain's totals, and everything else keeps showing the last chain that worked; leave the box (or press Enter) with the value still refused and it goes back to the last one that worked. A choice from a list that the budget refuses, such as an active combiner whose gains are listed for more levels than it has, is not made, and the reason is shown.

The system inputs

Input Meaning
Frequency The input (RF) frequency, in the frequency unit set in Settings ▸ General ▸ Units (GHz when that is Automatic). After a mixer the chain is at the difference frequency.
Bandwidth The noise bandwidth B the noise floor, the MDS and the SNR are read in.
Input power The signal at the input. In an array, at each element.
Source temperature The noise temperature of what drives the input, an antenna's for instance. 290 K is T0.
Required SNR What the demodulator needs: sensitivity is the MDS plus this.
Blockers Carriers at the input besides the signal: an offset from the frequency (MHz when bare) and a level, dBm, each pair separated by ; (150 MHz, -40; 20 MHz, -50). See Levels.
Direction Receive, the default, or Transmit: a chain driven at its input and read at its output. See Transmit chains.
RxOffset, RxBandwidth A transmit chain's receive band, where its output noise is read: its centre's offset from the carrier at the output and its width, MHz. Blank offset: none. Shown only when Direction is Transmit; a receive chain keeps the values.

Transfer to Schematic's drop-down has include a modulated-signal demo, which adds the demo bench to what it writes.

The stages, and the parts a stage can be

A stage has a name (its instance name on the schematic), a part, and that part's parameters. Nine parts are System blocks — the splitter and the array combiner are the library's Combiner, an active combiner that block with an Amplifier after each — and the library has no phase shifter, limiter, canceller or IQ modulator, so four more are composed of parts it does have. Transfer places exactly that composition. One more is data: an S-parameter data stage is a Touchstone file.

Part What it is Budget
Amplifier (Amp) The System Amplifier. Any gain, negative included: a block with a gain, an NF and an intercept is one. GainPerStage makes it ⌈Gain/GainPerStage⌉ amplifier stages, for its DC power. Law picks its compression: Tanh on IP3, or Rapp or Saleh on Psat (the laws). G = Gain, NF = NF (blank: noiseless), IIP3 from IP3 and IP3Ref, IP1dB = IIP3 − 8.96 dB; a Rapp or Saleh law's own
Mixer The System Mixer, down-converting to |f − Flo|, or with Sideband = Upper up-converting to f + Flo. Flo is the LO the bench drives it with, at Plo. G = ConvGain, NF = NF single-sideband (a DSB figure + 3.01 dB), IIP3 = IIP3, IP1dB = IIP3 − 8.96 dB
IQ modulator (IQMod, composed) Two Mixers fed in quadrature by a 90° Hybrid at the input, their LO split into its quadrature by a Combiner, summed by a second: an image-reject up-converter to Flo + f (Sideband Upper) or Flo − f, with GainImb, PhaseImb and each mixer's IsoLO_IF. See The IQ modulator. G = ConvGain + 20·log10(|1 + g·e^(jφ)|/2), NF a mixer's, IIP3 = IIP3 + 3.01 dB
Attenuator (Atten) A matched pad. G = −Loss, NF = Loss
Filter The synthesised Filter, in its passband. G = −IL, NF = IL; a Chebyshev's ripple is not in the budget
Switch A closed SPST switch. G = −IL, NF = IL
Isolator (Circulator) A circulator with its third port terminated. G = −IL, NF = IL
Directional coupler (Coupler) Its through arm, the coupled and isolated ports terminated. G = 10·log10(1 − 10^(−Coupling/10)) − IL, NF = −G
Phase shifter (composed) An Amplifier of gain −IL with NF and IIP3, and a TLIN of electrical length Phase. G = −IL, NF = NF (blank: IL), IIP3 = IIP3 (blank: linear)
Limiter (composed) An Amplifier of gain −IL, NF = IL, whose intercept puts its input 1 dB compression point at P1dB. G = −IL, NF = IL, IP1dB = P1dB
Canceller (composed) A Directional Coupler whose isolated port takes a reference path that subtracts a copy of an interference from the main path. See The canceller. G = −(IL − 10·log10(1 − c)), NF from the reference path's noise
N-way splitter The Combiner from its common port, one output followed and the others terminated. G = −(10·log10 N + IL), NF = −G
S-parameter data (SnP) A Touchstone file on the SnP block, read from port In to port Out. See S-parameter data. G = |S(Out,In)|² at the stage's frequency; NF from the file's noise data, or its own loss when passive; NF and IIP3 when stated
N-way array combiner The Combiner, every input an element's branch (or a sub-array's): one N:1, or a tree of 2:1s or of each level's own ways, passive or active. See Arrays, the variants and Sub-arrays. Direct, passive: signal +10·log10 N − IL, noise −IL, NF = IL

Every part also takes a Pdc, its DC power (W, or with its unit: 5 mW), which only the power readout reads; on an Amplifier with GainPerStage it is each amplifier stage's. Neither is written onto a bench.

P1dB follows from the intercept for every part that compresses, because an ideal Amplifier and Mixer have one nonlinearity, a tanh limiter, whose 1 dB compression point is IIP3 − 8.9625 dB. An Amplifier with a Rapp or Saleh law compresses as its law does instead. The budget uses the part's own law, so the simulation it is checked against compresses where the budget says.

S-parameter data

An S-parameter data stage puts a measured or simulated part into the chain as its Touchstone file: a filter, an LNA, a cable, a board. Pick the file with … beside File; a file inside the workspace is written relative to it, so the chain and its benches move with the workspace. Choosing the part asks for the file at once.

The file is interpolated to the frequency the stage sees — the chain's, or after a mixer the IF — exactly as the SnP block interpolates it in a simulation, and renormalised to 50 Ω if it is referenced to another impedance. A file with more than two ports is read from In to Out, every other port terminated in 50 Ω.

Quantity From the file
Gain |S(Out,In)|², between 50 Ω terminations
NF, from noise data A two-port read 1 → 2 with a noise block: its Fmin, Γopt and Rn at the stage's frequency (linear between rows, as the block takes them), at a 50 Ω source
NF, passive, no noise data Its own thermal noise: F = (1 − |S(Out,Out)|²) / |S(Out,In)|², its loss when matched
NF, with gain and no noise data Unknown: give NF
IIP3 IIP3; blank, linear

NF stated replaces the file's figure and may not be below it. On the benches a stated NF above the file's own, or a stated IIP3, is an ideal Amplifier of 0 dB after the block that carries the extra noise and the intercept, so the simulation still checks the stage.

The budget does not extrapolate. It refuses the chain, naming the stage, when:

  • no file is named, there is no file at the path, or the file is not Touchstone;
  • In or Out is not one of the file's ports, or both are the same port;
  • the stage's frequency is outside the file's frequencies, or outside its noise rows when the noise comes from them (state NF to use the file there);
  • the file has gain and no noise data, and NF is blank;
  • a relative path is given in a chain that has not been saved.

A blocker that reaches the stage outside the file's frequencies is carried at the file's nearest frequency, as the block holds it in a simulation, and the Notes say so.

Values that follow the frequency

A stage parameter that is a number may also be written as a value of the frequency, so a stage scales as the carrier moves and a frequency sweep shows it:

Written as Example Read
A number 8.5, 8.5 dB, 2.35 GHz as always
An expression 0.045*f_GHz + 1.29 in freq (Hz) or f_GHz (GHz), with the expression language's functions: log10, ceil, min, max, a < b ? x : y; a unit glued to its number, freq - 3GHz
A table lna_nf.csv a CSV file of freq,value rows (the frequency in Hz, or with its unit, 26 GHz; a first line that is not a row is its header), linear between rows

Each is read at its own stage's input frequency: the chain's, and after a mixer the IF. A mixer's Flo is read first, then the frequency moves, so Flo = freq - 3GHz keeps the IF at 3 GHz wherever the carrier is, and a filter's F1 = freq - 1.5GHz follows the carrier. The budget, the levels and every bench read the resulting number, the one the budget used, written in full: an ideal block on a schematic takes a number, not a function of the frequency.

A table is never extrapolated: a frequency outside its rows is a refusal that names the stage and the table's range. So is an expression that cannot be evaluated there (log10 of a negative number), or one that is not a real number. An expression that reads any name but freq and f_GHz is not a number, and is refused as one. A relative table path resolves from the workspace, as an SnP stage's file does.

The power-of-a-frequency forms a datasheet curve fit takes are one line each: a saturated power with a knee, freq < 30e9 ? 32.5 - 6*log10(f_GHz) : 45.79 - 15*log10(f_GHz); a loss rising with frequency, 0.012*f_GHz + 0.4; an amplifier stage's gain falling to 0 dB near the technology's limit, 33 - 15*log10(f_GHz).

What the cascade computes

Each row of the cascade is the chain up to and including that stage, referred to the chain's input. With G the available-power gains, T the noise temperatures and T0 = 290 K:

Quantity Formula
Gain G = Π gᵢ
Noise (Friis) Te = Σ Teᵢ / Gᵢ₋₁ with Teᵢ = T0·(Fᵢ − 1); F = 1 + Te/T0; NF = 10·log10 F
Each stage's share (Teᵢ / Gᵢ₋₁) / Te: the same split a noise run's NFpct reports
Intercept 1/IIP3 = Σ Gᵢ₋₁ / IIP3ᵢ (in mW); OIP3 = IIP3 + G
Compression 1/IP1dB = Σ Gᵢ₋₁ / IP1dBᵢ; OP1dB = IP1dB + G − 1 dB
Output power Pout = Pin + G
Thermal noise floor 10·log10(k·Ts·B) + 30 dBm, the source's own noise
Output noise 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·B·G) + 30 dBm
MDS 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·B) + 30 dBm: the input signal at 0 dB SNR
Sensitivity MDS + required SNR
SNR Pin − MDS
SFDR (2/3)·(IIP3 − MDS)

The intercept sum takes every stage's third-order products in phase, the worst case. For ideal blocks with real gains that is exactly what happens, and the two-tone simulation agrees to 2×10⁻⁴ dB. It takes each stage's products from the wanted signal alone: an amplifier right after a mixer, with no filter between them, also sees the mixer's sum product, and its third-order term mixes that with the IF onto the IF's own IM3, which the budget does not have (0.44 dB of IIP3 in the dual-conversion example without its roofing filter). The compression sum is an approximation of the same form: when two stages compress at similar levels the cascade compresses a little later than it predicts (see agreement).

A mixer's noise figure is its single-sideband one, and an SSB figure is stated with the image sideband terminated at T0. The budget also takes the image as filtered of every earlier stage's noise, which is what a preselector is for. That holds when the image filter is right in front of the mixer: a stage between them, an amplifier say, puts its own noise at the image, which the budget does not have. To see how much of an image a chain rejects, give it a blocker at the image's offset: the levels carry it through each filter's own response and each mixer, and its level at the output, against the signal's, is the chain's rejection of that image.

Transmit chains

Direction ▸ Transmit reads the same cascade from its other end. The input is the drive — the complex IF a DAC delivers, say — and the chain ends at the antenna. Every stage, every row and every number of the cascade is the same as a receive chain's; the totals add the transmitter's own, and leave out a receiver's sensitivity and range:

Readout Formula
Output power Pout = Pin + G, the linear budget's
Output, CW the carrier through every stage's compression in turn: a Rapp or Saleh stage its law's AM-AM, every other stage that compresses its tanh limiter's describing function, N(u) = (2/πu)·∫₀^π tanh(u·cos θ)·cos θ dθ at u = 2·√(P/IIP3)
Back-off from OP1dB OP1dB − Pout, the cascade's OP1dB
Psat, and the back-off from it the output's ceiling, P_k = min(P_(k−1) + g_k, Psat_k) through the stages, Psat_k a stage's own (a tanh stage's OIP3 − 10·log10(π²/4), 3.92 dB under it); Psat − Pout
ACLR 2·(Pout − OIP3) − 10·log10 3, dBc: below
Noise floor 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·G) + 30, dBm/Hz at the output
Noise in the receive band the same sum with every stage's gain at the band's frequency, a filter passing |S21|² there and adding T0·(1 − |S21|² − |S22|²): dBm/Hz, and dBm in the band
Image, LO an IQ modulator's, each carried to the output through every stage at its own frequency, dBc

The ACLR relation, and what it assumes. Take a memoryless nonlinearity to third order on the complex envelope, y = a₁x + a₃x|x|², driven by a signal x that is complex Gaussian with power P and a flat spectrum of width B — OFDM is close to one, by the central limit theorem. By Isserlis' theorem (L. Isserlis, "On a formula for the product-moment coefficient of any order of a normal frequency distribution in any number of variables", Biometrika, 1918, and for a complex Gaussian I. S. Reed, "On a moment theorem for complex Gaussian processes", IRE Transactions on Information Theory, 1962), E|x|⁴ = 2P² and E|x|⁶ = 6P³, so the third-order output's part correlated with x is a gain change, 2a₃P·x, and the rest, of power 2|a₃|²P³, spreads as the threefold convolution of the flat spectrum over 3B: two thirds of it in the channel and a sixth in each neighbour of the same width, one bandwidth away. The two-tone intercept of the same nonlinearity is IIP3 = |a₁/a₃| per tone, so the neighbour holds |a₃|²P³/3 against |a₁|²P in the channel:

ACLR = (P/IIP3)² / 3      →      ACLR = 2·(Pout − OIP3) − 4.77 dB

It assumes third order dominates, a back-off well under compression; a noise-like signal; the neighbour the signal's width at one bandwidth's offset (an NR carrier is measured over its occupied bandwidth at the channel spacing, 98.28 MHz at 100 MHz for a 100 MHz carrier, which moves the sixth to 0.158, 0.23 dB); and every stage's IM3 in phase, as the cascade's intercept takes them. Two equal tones at the same total power put each IM3 product at 2·(Pout − 3.01 − OIP3), 1.25 dB under the relation's ACLR. The relation is an estimate: the linear transmitter shows how far it holds with a real PA law.

The receive band. A transmitter's own noise at a receiver's frequency — a duplex offset, a receiver beside it — is what its band filter must remove. Give the band's offset from the carrier at the output, and its width: the noise there is the Friis sum again with each stage's gain at that frequency. A filter's is its own response, and its noise is Bosma's: it passes |S21|² of what arrives and adds T0·(1 − |S21|² − |S22|² ), its loss in its passband but almost nothing in its stopband, where it reflects rather than dissipates; a reflected wave is the stage before's to absorb.

A converter's sideband. A Mixer goes on at its difference, |f − Flo|, by default; Sideband = Upper takes its sum, f + Flo, as an up-converter does. The budget's numbers are the same either way, since an ideal multiplier puts the same conversion gain into both; the frequency the chain goes on at, every stage after it reads, and the bench tracks, moves. The bench's filter after a mixer is what removes the other sideband.

A transmit chain has no link in front of it: a link's transmitter feeds a receive chain.

The amplifier's laws

An Amplifier's Law picks how it compresses, in the budget and in the simulation alike:

Law Gain against the input power s IP1dB Psat IIP3 the budget uses
Tanh (the default) the soft limiter on the instantaneous input IIP3 − 8.9625 dB OIP3 − 3.92 dB IP3's, its own third-order term
Rapp (1 + (s/P0)P)(−1/(2P)), P0 = Psat/G P0 + (10/P)·log10(10^(P/10) − 1) Psat, its asymptote the cubic's with its 1 dB point: IP1dB + 9.64 dB
Saleh e^(jΦ(v)) / (1 + v), Φ(v) = a·v/(1 + b·v), v = s/s_sat, s_sat = 4·Psat/G s_sat + 10·log10(10^(1/20) − 1), Psat − G − 3.12 dB Psat, the AM-AM's peak, 6.02 dB into compression its own third-order term, AM-PM in it: s_sat − 5·log10(1 + a²)

P is Rapp's smoothness: at 1 the 1 dB point is 5.87 dB under the saturated input, at 2 1.16 dB, at 3 0.01 dB, a hard clip's. Saleh's phase is stated by its value at the drive that saturates it, PhiSat, and its limit, PhiMax, beyond it on the same side of zero: b = PhiSat/(PhiMax − PhiSat), a = PhiMax·b; both 0 is no AM-PM. The laws are

  1. Rapp, "Effects of HPA-nonlinearity on 4-DPSK/OFDM-signal for a digital sound broadcasting system", Proceedings of the 2nd European Conference on Satellite Communications, 1991, and A. A. M. Saleh, "Frequency-independent and frequency-dependent nonlinear models of TWT amplifiers", IEEE Transactions on Communications, 1981, here with the amplifier's own gain and a saturated power in place of their normalised constants.

What Rapp's intercept is. Rapp's law has no third-order term unless P is 1: at small drive its IM3 rises 2P + 1 dB for every dB, and no intercept describes it. The budget gives it the cubic's with the same small-signal gain and the same 1 dB point — the textbook IP3 = P1dB + 9.64 dB — which is what an intercept sum and an ACLR estimate can take. At P = 1 its own third-order term is 0.76 dB lower. For P = 2 the cubic is pessimistic for two tones away from compression: at the linear transmitter's operating point their IM3 reads 4.1 dB under it, and 20 dB further down the PA's products fall at five times the drive. It is optimistic for a noise-like carrier at the same point: the NR carrier's peaks reach past the 1 dB point, where Rapp's law clips harder than the cubic, and the PA alone reads its ACLR 0.8 dB worse than the estimate.

How the simulation does it. A Rapp or Saleh law is a bandpass law, stated for a narrowband signal's envelope, so the amplifier applies it to its input's analytic signal: the input voltage and its quadrature, which a linear companion holds on a net of its own at the input's Hilbert transform (see System Components ▸ Amplifier). One tone's envelope is constant, so a one-tone run reads the law at that drive exactly, and nothing at the harmonics; two tones beat, and their products are the law's own. Every analysis carries it: single- and multi-tone harmonic balance, the envelope, and an S-parameter run, where the law is its gain. A transmit chain's PA bench reads its AM-AM and AM-PM over the drive against the closed forms: 6.5×10⁻¹⁰ dB and 10⁻¹⁵°, and its 1 dB point to the three-point interpolation's 0.01 dB.

The IQ modulator

An IQMod stage is an image-reject up-converter of library blocks, placed as Transfer places every composed stage:

Part Placed as
The input's quadrature a 90° Hybrid (a Coupler of 3.01 dB at 90°), its fourth port terminated: the I arm and the Q arm
The LO a P1Tone at Flo, 3.01 dB over Plo so each mixer is driven at its stated Plo, split by a 2-way Combiner whose second path is at +90° (the upper sideband) or −90°, plus PhaseImb
The mixers two Mixers of ConvGain, NF, IIP3 and IsoLO_IF, the Q one's gain ConvGain + GainImb
The sum a 2-way Combiner

The LO's split is a Combiner rather than a second hybrid because its path phase is flat and it stays passive at any phase; a hybrid set off quadrature does not. With g = 10^(GainImb/20) and φ = PhaseImb, against one balanced mixer the wanted sideband comes out at |1 + g·e^(jφ)|²/4 and its image at |1 − g·e^(jφ)|²/4:

Quantity Closed form
Gain ConvGain + 20·log10(|1 + g·e^(jφ)|/2): ConvGain when balanced
Image rejection |1 + g·e^(jφ)|² / |1 − g·e^(jφ)|²: 35.17 dB at 0.2 dB and 1.5°, which is what an uncalibrated modulator achieves
LO at its output Plo − IsoLO_IF + 10·log10(1 ∓ sin φ), each mixer's feedthrough, the two in quadrature, summed at half each
IIP3, IP1dB a mixer's, 3.01 dB up: each mixer takes half the input
NF a mixer's single-sideband figure

The image is at Flo ∓ f and the LO at Flo; the readouts carry each through the stages after the modulator at its own frequency, so a band filter's rejection of them is in the numbers at the output. Its input is the chain's frequency, the IF the modulator up-converts — high enough, for a wide carrier, that the LO and the image clear the adjacent channels: the linear transmitter's 200 MHz puts them 200 and 400 MHz below a 100 MHz carrier.

Arrays: N elements into a combiner

A Combiner stage makes the chain an array. Every stage before it is one element's branch, repeated N times; the stages after it are the one receiver the elements are combined into. Every number is then referred to one element's input, and the input power is per element.

  • Signal from the N branches arrives in phase and adds in amplitude: the combiner's signal gain is +10·log10 N − IL.
  • Noise from the N branches is uncorrelated and adds in power: the combiner's noise gain is −IL only. The array's noise temperature is therefore one branch's Friis sum, with the combiner's excess loss as a pad, and its NF is one element's.
  • SNR rises by 10·log10 N, the array gain: SNR = Pin + 10·log10 N − 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·B) − 30. The MDS and sensitivity per element fall by the same amount.
  • Intercepts after the combiner see N times one element's power, so the intercept and compression points referred to one element fall by 10·log10 N for the stages after it, and the output-referred ones rise.

Steer is the phase step of the arriving wave between adjacent elements. Transfer draws the wave's extra path to element k as a line of (k − 1)·Steer in front of it, and sets element k's phase shifter to Phase + (N − k)·Steer, which brings every element to the combiner in phase. Without a phase shifter before the combiner a non-zero Steer misaligns the elements, and the budget says so: its coherent sum assumes they are aligned. A phase shifter after a mixer whose LO is above the signal works on an IF whose phase is the RF's negated, so there it is set to Phase + (k − 1)·Steer instead; Transfer follows each element's spectrum through the chain and picks the one that aligns it.

The combiner's variants

A Combiner stage is one of four, chosen by two parameters:

Kind = Passive Kind = Active
Topology = Direct one N:1 combiner of loss IL the N:1 combiner, then an amplifier of Gain, NF and IIP3
Topology = Tree levels of 2:1 combiners (or each level's Ways), each of loss IL, a remainder passed through each level's combiners each followed by an amplifier
Topology = Levels one N:1 combiner, any N, with the loss of the ⌈log2 N⌉ levels a tree would take: ⌈log2 N⌉·IL that combiner, then an amplifier

Levels is a tree's loss for any number of elements, which a receive array swept over 6 or 11 elements needs: an ideal N-way sum through ⌈log2 N⌉ lossy levels. It is transferred as one N:1 combiner of that loss, which its benches check as they check a direct one. A real tree of 6 is a Tree, with its unequal paths (see Sub-arrays).

Parameter Meaning
N The number of elements: any, for every topology.
Topology Direct, Tree or Levels.
Ways Tree only: each level's ways, the first level (next to the elements) first, 2, 3. Blank: 2 at every level, ⌈log2 N⌉ of them. Level by level the inputs go into parts of that many; a remainder of one is passed through, of more a smaller part. The ways must bring the N inputs to one output.
Kind Passive or Active.
IL Each combiner's loss above the ideal split, dB. A tree takes one value for every level, or one per level, the first level (next to the elements) first: 0.3, 0.4.
PathIL Each input path's own extra loss, N values, dB — an amplitude taper, or an imbalance. Passive or active; in an active combiner each level's amplifier then sees its own path's power. Blank: none.
Gain, NF, IIP3 Active only: each combiner's amplifier; one value, or one per level. Its 1 dB compression point is its intercept's, IIP3 − 8.96 dB, as every amplifier's here.
Steer The arriving wave's phase step between elements (see above).

Each variant's budget follows every path through its own levels, and every number is referred to one element's input:

  • The element paths first. With amplitudes a_k = 10^(−PathIL_k/20), element k enters with amplitude a_k, noise gain a_k² and, its weight being a matched pad at T0, T0·(1 − a_k²) of noise.
  • Then each part of each level: a passive part of n inputs and loss L sums their amplitudes times √(1/(n·L)), their noise gains and noise temperatures times 1/(n·L), and adds T0·(1 − 1/L) of its own; a part of one input passes it through. An active level's amplifier follows each part with its own gain, noise figure and intercept, and its third-order product, (its input amplitude)³ over its IIP3, adds in phase with every other amplifier's.
  • At the output: the signal gain is the coherent amplitude squared, the noise gain the summed noise gains, the NF from the noise temperature over the noise gain, and the IIP3 the amplitude over the third-order sum. The array gain is the signal gain over the noise gain, (Σt_k)²/Σt_k² with t_k each element's own amplitude to the output: N for equal paths, less with a taper or an uneven tree.
  • With equal paths every part of a level sees the same, and this is the cascade of the levels exactly as a chain's: Friis with the noise gains, the intercept sum with the signal gains. The amplifiers of one level are in parallel, each fed by its own part, and identical, so together they behave as one amplifier seeing the combined power.

So a passive tree's loss accumulates level by level, and its noise figure is its whole loss; a direct combiner has one loss. An active combiner's noise figure is set by its first level, and its intercept by its last, which sees the most power: in the example's array, the active tree's IIP3 is 7 dB below the direct active combiner's.

The example's array, the same four elements into each variant (IL 0.5 dB, the amplifiers 10 dB, NF 2 dB, IIP3 10 dBm), at the combiner's output and per element:

Variant Gain NF IIP3 OIP3 Array gain
Direct, passive 18.52 dB 1.33 dB −9.19 dBm 9.33 dBm 6.02 dB
Tree, passive 18.02 dB 1.35 dB −9.19 dBm 8.83 dBm 6.02 dB
Direct, active 28.52 dB 1.43 dB −11.88 dBm 16.64 dBm 6.02 dB
Tree, active 38.02 dB 1.45 dB −18.77 dBm 19.26 dBm 6.02 dB

Sub-arrays, uneven trees and unequal paths

A chain may have more than one Combiner. The stages before the first are one element's branch, those between two Combiners one sub-array's, and those after the last the receiver. Every number is still referred to one element's input: each Combiner adds its own signal and noise gains to the cascade, and the array gain is the product of each one's. The array has as many elements as the Combiners' N multiplied, and the DC power counts each stage as many times as the array has it. Steer is the step between adjacent elements, across the whole array, and is the first Combiner's; a later Combiner's is 0. A later Combiner's PathIL weights its sub-arrays. The RxElements sweep sizes a chain of one Combiner only.

A tree takes any N. Level by level its inputs go into parts of Ways inputs each (2 at every level when blank); when they do not divide, a remainder of one is passed through, with no combiner and no loss, and a remainder of more is a smaller part. Three elements in 2:1 levels are a 2:1 and a pass-through, then a 2:1; six in Ways = 2, 3 are three 2:1s, then a 3:1. An uneven tree loses coherence: the pass-through and a combined pair reach the next equal-split combiner with unequal amplitudes, and N unequal inputs sum to less than their total power. Three elements into a lossless 2:1 tree give (1 + 1/√2)² = 2.91 times one element's power, not 3, an array gain of 4.65 dB instead of 4.77 dB, while their noise, uncorrelated, keeps its whole power. The budget follows each path (see the variants), so it has this, and the benches show it.

An active combiner takes a taper too. With PathIL, each level's amplifier sees its own path's power: the amplifier after a strong pair compresses first, and the combiner's IIP3 is the in-phase sum of every amplifier's third-order product, each at its own input power.

The example's IF Array.cchain has all three: six elements, each an LNA (18 dB, NF 1.2 dB, OIP3 10 dBm), a preselector, a mixer to 350 MHz, an IF filter and a phase shifter at the IF; two sub-arrays of three, each an active tree with a pass-through (0.5 dB, the amplifiers 10 dB, NF 2 dB, IIP3 10 dBm, PathIL = 1, 0, 1) and a sub-array amplifier; and a 2:1 combiner of the two, then an IF amplifier. Per element:

Stage Its own gain NF IIP3 Cumulative gain NF Array gain
LNA, RFBPF, MIX, IFBPF, PS 5.50 dB 2.00 dB
SUB, 3 into a tree 23.15 dB 3.19 dB −3.41 dBm 28.65 dB 2.77 dB 4.64 dB
SA, × 2 10 dB 3 dB OIP3 25 dBm 38.65 dB 2.77 dB 4.64 dB
ARR, 2 into one 2.71 dB 0.30 dB 41.36 dB 2.77 dB 7.65 dB
IFA 10 dB 4 dB OIP3 30 dBm 51.36 dB 2.78 dB 7.65 dB

The whole: IIP3 −22.53 dBm, IP1dB −31.49 dBm, MDS −112.32 dBm in 4.5 MHz, SNR 32.32 dB at −80 dBm, SFDR 59.86 dB. The array gain is 7.65 dB of six elements' 7.78: 0.13 dB to the sub-array's pass-through and its taper. The pair's amplifier in each sub-array sees 3.0 dB more than the pass-through's. The IF filter is in each element, right after its mixer: the sub-array's amplifiers are broadband, and without it they see the mixer's sum product at 4.55 GHz as well as the IF, and the chain compresses 0.22 dB before its budget.

Transfer places each Combiner once for each copy the array has of it, and a sub-array's stages once a sub-array, named SA_1, SA_2; a pass-through is a wire, or an Atten when its path has a loss. The block view draws the branch once, marked × 6, and the sub-array's stages once, marked × 2.

A link in front of the chain

On the Link tab, a transmitter and a path in front of the chain adds a transmit array and a line-of-sight path: the power they deliver to each receive element becomes the chain's input power, and the receive array is the chain's own Combiner (one element with none). The transmitter and the path are not stages, because a stage before the combiner is one receive element's branch and every number is referred to that element's input. Each input but Elements and Distance may be a number, an expression or a table, read at the carrier.

Transmitter Meaning
Psat Each transmit element's PA saturated output, dBm.
Backoff Its output back-off: Pout = Psat − Backoff. The TX bench shows what a back-off costs in EVM and ACPR.
Loss From each PA to its antenna element (a switch, a line), dB.
AntennaGain Each transmit element's gain, dBi.
Elements Mtx, the transmit elements, all in phase toward the receiver.
PaGain, PAE, Pdc For the DC power: the PA's gain and its power-added efficiency at the back-off, %, or each element's DC power stated.
Path Meaning
Distance The path: metres, or with m or km (200 m, 0.2 km).
Attenuation Extra or atmospheric attenuation along it, dB/km: a number, an expression or a table of the carrier.
RxAntennaGain Each receive element's gain, dBi. 
Pout = Psat − Backoff
EIRP = Pout − Loss + AntennaGain + 20·log10(Mtx)           Mtx PAs in phase: Mtx of power, Mtx of directivity
Lfs  = 20·log10(4π·d·f / c)                                 free space
A    = Attenuation · d / 1000
Prx  = EIRP − Lfs − A + RxAntennaGain                       at each receive element
Pin  = min(Prx, IP1dB − RxBackoff)                          the chain's input

The receiver's ceiling. A link that delivers more than the receiver takes is held at its input P1dB less RxBackoff (10 dB), as power control or a variable gain would hold it, and the Notes say so. Without a link the input is not moved, and the Notes say when it is above that ceiling. Which stage sets the compression is in the cascade table's P1dB share column, each stage's share of 1/IP1dB; when the largest share is after the combiner the Notes name it. That is the common case in an array: the elements' signals reach a mixer after the combiner in phase, N times one element's power, so a mixer compresses long before any element's LNA does.

The combiner convention. A Combiner here is a matched N:1 network: N in-phase element signals come out at N times one element's power, their noise once. Some analyses count the in-phase sum in voltage instead, 20·log10 N of signal and 10·log10 N of noise. The SNR, and every readout below, is the same either way; the absolute level after the combiner differs by 10·log10 N.

EIRP and the path have no circuit to simulate; the benches run the receiver at the power the link delivers, and the closed forms above are checked against an independent calculation, testdata/chain/link_reference.py.

SNR, rate, DC power and the NF allowance

Every chain, with a link or without, reads as a receiver of data. The Receiver row of the Link tab holds the inputs:

Input Meaning
FBW A fractional bandwidth: B = FBW · frequency (0.1 for 10 %), which then replaces the Bandwidth input, for the noise too. Blank: the Bandwidth input.
Streams Orthogonal streams (two polarisations, MIMO layers), each with its own hardware: the rate and the DC power both multiply by it, and the energy per bit does not move.
NfAllowance The NF allowance's step, dB (1).
RxBackoff The receiver's ceiling below its input P1dB, dB (10).
Readout Formula
Noise at the input the MDS, 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·B) + 30 − 10·log10(A): kTB and the array's NF
NF of the array 10·log10(F/A), F the per-element noise factor and A the array gain; in linear terms F/A = F_A/M + (F_B − 1)/G_A for equal paths and F_A/A + (F_B − 1)/G_A with a PathIL taper: F_A the front end's to the combiner's output, F_B the stages after it, G_A the gain to that output with the array gain; below 0 dB for a large array
SNR, margin Pin − MDS; SNR − required SNR
Rate S · B · log2(1 + 10^(SNR/10)), Shannon's capacity over S streams
PA DC power (Pout − Pout/G) / PAE, at the back-off, unless the transmitter's Pdc is stated
DC power S · (Mtx · P_PA + Mrx · Σ P_branch + Σ P_after): the branch's stages once per receive element, the combiner and every stage after it once
Energy per bit DC power / rate
NF allowed after a stage 10·log10(1 + F_k·(10^(X/10) − 1)·Gn_k), X the allowance: the largest NF the rest of the chain may have for the whole to stay within X dB of the NF up to stage k (F_k and Gn_k its cumulative noise factor and noise gain)

The NF left column of the cascade table is the last of these: after the example's LNA, the rest of the chain may have an NF of 16.7 dB and cost the chain 1 dB. It is what tells how much gain an LNA needs before a noisy mixer.

Sweeps

The Sweeps row of the Link tab takes up to three sweeps, each one line, as the Blockers are:

Sweep Line Points
Frequency 20 GHz, 40 GHz, 41 carriers evenly from the first to the last
TxElements 4, 1024, 9 transmit array sizes spread evenly in ratio, each rounded to a whole element and kept once
RxElements 1, 64, 13 the receive Combiner's N, the same way; 1 is one element with no combiner

Each point is the whole chain budgeted again there, every expression and table read at that point's carrier. Each sweep has its own tab: the link levels (EIRP, the received power at each element, the chain's input, the ceiling and the noise, the MDS), the SNR and margin, the rate and the DC power, over its own axis, a log one for an array's sizes. A point the budget refuses (a table read outside its range) is left out, and one note gives how many and why; a carrier where a Filter's passband no longer holds the stage's frequency is noted, since the budget takes its loss there and not its roll-off.

A sweep is not a bench: transfer the chain at a point (set the frequency, or Elements, or N) and its benches check that point. circuitrf chain -o writes each sweep as a group of the DataSet, named after it (Frequency.SNR_dB).

Transfer to Schematic

Transfer to Schematic saves the chain and writes its test-bench cells beside the .cchain, named after it, each with a Data Display of the same name that Simulate opens on the bench's own result. Every chain gets 1-Tone, 2-Tone, Envelope and Levels; a chain with blockers a Blockers bench; a chain with a canceller a Canceller bench; an array Steering (when the branch has a phase shifter) and Combiners, as harmonic balance when the branch has a mixer; and, when asked, the Demo. A chain with more than one mixer gets most of them once per conversion:

Bench Source Analyses Measures
<chain> 1-Tone a P1Tone per element (port 1 … N), a Port at the output without a mixer, an S-parameter run with Noise=yes; with one, harmonic-balance noise with the LO running. And a harmonic-balance drive sweep at the predicted IP1dB gain, NF, each stage's cumulative NF from the run's own shares, IP1dB, OP1dB
<chain> 2-Tone a PnTone per element, 1 MHz apart, 50 dB below the predicted IIP3 multi-tone harmonic balance gain, IIP3, OIP3, and each stage's gain and OIP3 at its output
<chain> Envelope a MOD_Source per element: an NR carrier, its source noisy at the source temperature envelope with Noise=yes and EvmSplit=yes in-channel SNR, the EVM's noise part, output power and output noise
<chain> Steering a plane wave: one Port into a Combiner used as a splitter, path k delayed by the wave's extra path; the elements and the combiners, level by level, a Port at the last one's output an S-parameter run with Noise=yes in a sweep of theta_in (−90° to 90°) within a sweep of theta_steer (−30°, 0°, 30°); through a mixer, harmonic balance with one LO split to every mixer, theta_in in 5° steps, and a noise run at each beam's peak the pattern against the arriving angle beside the closed-form array factor; at each beam's peak the gain, the NF and the array gain. See Steering
<chain> Combiners the same elements into each of the four variants of the first combiner (one sub-array's in sub-arrays), each fed by its own wave at broadside one S-parameter run with Noise=yes; through a mixer, one harmonic-balance noise run a variant, the LO split to every mixer each variant's gain and NF, beside its budget, intercepts and array gain
<chain> Levels a PnTone per element, two tones 1 MHz apart, each at the input power multi-tone harmonic balance, on the 2-Tone bench's mixing order the signal and its IM3 at every node. See Levels
<chain> Blockers a PnTone per element with every blocker, an isolator after every stage harmonic balance every blocker at every node
<chain> Canceller the canceller on its own: a wanted signal and an interference from MOD_Sources envelope runs, swept the depth against each error, the wanted signal's EVM, SNR and constellation with and without cancellation. See The canceller
<chain> Demo a MOD_Source of NR 64-QAM and one of DBPSK per element; the LO with a phase-noise mask envelope with Noise=yes and EvmSplit=yes, the input power swept the constellation, the EVM against the input power, its noise and distortion parts. See The demo
<chain> TX a chain with a link: one transmit element's PA, an NR 64-QAM carrier from a MOD_Source, through its Loss envelope, swept over the back-off from Psat the output against the budget's Pout − Loss, the EVM and the adjacent-channel ratios. See The TX bench

The chain's parts are placed as written. Three things are the bench's and not the chain's:

  • the sources, the load and each mixer's LO, a P1Tone at Flo and Plo;
  • an isolator in front of each mixer (a Circulator whose third port is terminated at the ambient). It terminates the mixer's image at T0, the termination its SSB noise figure is stated against. A filter in front of a mixer reflects the image instead, and the mixer's noise then differs: in the superhet example the harmonic-balance noise figure reads 0.28 dB higher without the isolator. Delete it to see what your own image termination does;
  • in an array, the arriving wave's path: a TLIN of (k − 1)·Steer in front of element k (on the Steering and Combiners benches, the splitter's own path phases instead).

Every bench sets temp = 16.85, which puts every part at 290 K, the temperature a noise figure is stated at. Each row of its MEAS block reads one analysis, so circuitrf hb … -a SW1 evaluates the compression rows on its own. The envelope SNR is measured over the NR carrier's occupied bandwidth (the 15 kHz-spacing channel nearest the chain's bandwidth), and its prediction beside it is computed in that bandwidth.

An array's 1-Tone bench has N + 1 ports. Its gain is |Σₖ S(N+1, k)|², which is the budget's only if every phase shifter removes its element's steering, and its NF is one element's: F = 1 + (F₁ − 1)·|S(N+1, 1)|²/Σₖ|S(N+1, k)|², where F₁ is the noise factor from port 1 with the other elements' terminations noiseless — F = 1 + (F₁ − 1)/N for equal paths.

A transmit chain's benches

A transmit chain is driven at its input and read at its output, so its benches are its own:

Bench Source Analyses Measures
<chain> 1-Tone a P1Tone at the input (port 1), a Port at the output harmonic balance swept over the drive from 20 dB under the input power to 10 dB past the back-off from Psat, with the predicted IP1dB ± 0.25 dB in it; harmonic-balance noise at the input power, 1 MHz off the carrier and in the receive band the output against the drive beside the budget's CW output; the 1 dB point; the noise floor and the receive band's; an IQ modulator's image and LO at its own output and at the chain's
<chain> 2-Tone a PnTone of two tones 1 MHz apart, their total the input power multi-tone harmonic balance at three levels: 20 dB and 6 dB under, and at, the input power the IM3 against the level beside the intercept's 2·(P + G − OIP3); the intercept 20 dB down
<chain> Envelope a MOD_Source at the input: an NR 64-QAM carrier, noiseless envelope at the input power and 3 dB either side the output power beside the linear budget, the ACLR beside the budget's estimate, the EVM, the spectrum
<chain> PA the PA stage alone, from a MOD_Source at its own input and frequency harmonic balance swept over its drive (a MOD_Source is a CW carrier there), and an envelope run at its input power AM-AM and AM-PM beside its law's closed forms, its 1 dB point and saturation, its efficiency; the NR carrier's ACLR and EVM through it

The PA is the chain's last Amplifier with a Rapp or Saleh law, else its last that compresses. An ideal amplifier draws its stated Pdc at every drive, so its efficiency is the power it adds over that: class A's shape, 50 % at saturation for a Pdc of twice Psat. The NR carrier is the 15 kHz-spacing channel nearest the chain's bandwidth up to 50 MHz, as a receive chain's, and the 30 kHz one above it (up to 100 MHz, 273 resource blocks).

The 1-Tone bench puts an isolator after an IQ modulator, the bench's and not the chain's: the filter after it reflects the image and the LO, and a node in front of a reflection reads the incident wave plus the reflected one; behind the isolator the modulator's output reads the wave going forward, as the Blockers bench's nodes do. Every bench is checked before it is written, as a receive chain's are: an IQ modulator's LO is a tone, so the 1-Tone run has two tones, the 2-Tone run three, each at the order its numbers converge at or the highest under the 600-product cap; the envelope run has two fundamentals, the carrier's and the LO's, the LO more than three bandwidths from it.

The TX bench

The TX bench is one transmit element: an NR 64-QAM carrier into an Amplifier of PaGain whose output intercept is Psat + 10·log10(π²/4) = Psat + 3.92 dB — the tanh limiter saturates its fundamental that far below its intercept — then the transmitter's Loss as an Attenuator, into 50 Ω. An envelope run is swept over the back-off BO from 10 dB of overdrive to 16 dB back, and the link's own, with the drive Pin = Psat − BO − PaGain. Its display: the output at the antenna against the budget's Psat − BO − Loss, their difference, the EVM and the two adjacent-channel ratios against the back-off, and a table at the link's back-off.

The budget takes the PA's output as Psat − Backoff; the bench shows what that leaves out. The ideal PA is soft, its 1 dB compression point 6 dB below Psat, and an NR carrier's peaks reach it: in the example at 8 dB of back-off the output is 0.92 dB below Psat − 8 dB and the EVM 6.3 %, at 12 dB 0.41 dB and 2.9 %. Choose the back-off for the EVM and ACPR the link needs, from this table. A memoryless PA's EVM and ACPR do not depend on the bandwidth, so the bench's NR carrier is the 15 kHz-spacing channel nearest the chain's bandwidth, 50 MHz at most; the subcarrier spacing changes neither the budget nor what a memoryless block does to a carrier's EVM.

More than one conversion

Every bench Transfer writes is checked against what its runs take: a harmonic-balance run at most six tones and 600 mixing products, its noise run one or two tones, and an envelope run two fundamentals, the carrier's and one LO's, with the LO more than three of the carrier's bandwidths from it. Each LO is a tone of its own, so a chain with two mixers outgrows them: its 1-Tone bench's noise run would have three tones, and its envelope runs three fundamentals.

Such a chain is checked once per conversion. Conversion k runs from the stage after mixer k − 1 (from the input, for the first) to mixer k (to the output, for the last), so each holds one mixer and the filtering in front of it. Its benches are named after the IF it ends at, <chain> IF1 1-Tone, <chain> IF2 1-Tone and so on, and each is the chain from that point on:

  • driven at the IF the conversion before it ends at, at the budget's level there, with every blocker as it arrives there;
  • from a source whose temperature is the noise the stages before it deliver, (Ts + Te)·Gn, so that its SNR and its noise floor at every node are the whole chain's;
  • beside its own budget: its gain, NF and intercepts are those of its own stages, and the whole chain's follow from them by the same sums, F = F₁ + (F₂ − 1)/G₁ and 1/IIP3 = 1/IIP3₁ + G₁/IIP3₂.

A bench one run can hold is still written for the whole chain, at a lower mixing order when the cap needs it. A dual-conversion chain's 2-Tone bench is one: four tones (the two, and both LOs) at MaxMixOrder 5, the least that carries the output's IM3, retain 341 mixing products, where the 7 its IF stages converge at would retain 1,121. Transfer says so, and the intercepts read 3×10⁻³ dB high (agreement). A run of the whole chain also sees what a conversion's bench, fed a clean IF, cannot: the cross-products of the cascade's note. The 1-Tone, Levels and Blockers benches go per conversion together, since the Levels display reads all three node by node. In the window the Levels tab then shows the budget's lines, and each conversion's display its simulated points.

A bench no run can hold even per conversion is not written, and both Transfer and circuitrf check say why (in check, a chain.bench.left-out warning). Two causes besides too many tones or products:

  • An LO within three bandwidths of the envelope's carrier. The Envelope and Demo benches send an NR carrier near the chain's bandwidth, 5 MHz for 4.5 MHz. A second IF of 10.7 MHz puts the second LO 10.7 MHz from that carrier at the first IF, and the second conversion's Envelope and Demo benches are left out; a second IF of 21.4 MHz runs.
  • Two products on one frequency, one of them read. A blocker exactly on a mixer's image converts to exactly where another tone's product lands, and a harmonic-balance run cannot tell the two apart. Move the blocker a little off the image, as the example's second blocker is. Two products the bench reads neither of do not stop it: blockers spaced evenly put their differences on one frequency, and the bench runs, a few thousandths of a dB off, and says so. An envelope run takes no coincidence at all: an LO at two thirds of the signal puts the IF on a second product too.

Steering the beam in simulation

The Steering bench is the array at the combiner, fed by a plane wave and steered from its own VAR block:

Variable Meaning
theta_in The arriving wave's angle from broadside, degrees. The bench sweeps it from −90° to 90° in 1° steps.
theta_steer The angle the phase shifters steer to, degrees. The bench sweeps −30°, 0° and 30°.
d_over_lambda The element spacing in wavelengths, 0.5.
taper An amplitude taper, dB: the two edge elements' paths lose taper more, the others a share in proportion to their distance from the centre. 0.
psi_in, dphi 360°·d/λ·sin θ for the wave and for the steer: the phase step between adjacent elements.

The wave is one Port into a Combiner used as a splitter, whose path k has the phase −(k − 1)·psi_in: element k receives the wave (k − 1) element spacings later. Each element's phase shifter advances it by (k − 1)·dphi (its line is (k − 1)·(360° − dphi) long, the same phase at the bench's frequency and never a negative length), and the taper sits on the combiner's paths. Because the splitter shares the wave's power equally and its own isolation network is noisy at T0, each element sees an equal share of the signal and its own, uncorrelated, thermal noise, as an element of a real array does from its own antenna.

Its display plots the pattern, the simulated gain over the budget's peak gain at the combiner, against theta_in for each steer angle, and beside it the closed-form array factor:

AF(θ_in) = | Σₖ a_k · e^(−j·(k − 1)·(ψ_in − ψ_steer)) | / Σₖ a_k,      ψ = 2π·(d/λ)·sin θ

with a_k each path's amplitude weight (its PathIL and the taper). Each peak sits at its steer angle, and there the table reads the gain, the NF from the wave's port and the array gain, 10·log10 N less what the NF says it costs over one element's own: 6.02 dB for four equal elements, at every steer angle, with the NF unmoved. With a taper the main lobe widens and the sidelobes fall, and both the pattern and the closed form lose the taper's coherent loss at the peak. Change d_over_lambda to 1 and the grating lobes appear at ±90°.

Edit a sweep's values, or delete the sweeps and set theta_in and theta_steer by hand: everything is an ordinary variable.

Through a mixer no S-parameter run reaches the combiner, so the bench is harmonic balance: the wave is a P1Tone of Pw, 40 dB under the array's compression, every mixer of a stage is driven from one LO, a P1Tone into a Combiner used as a splitter at Plo plus the split, and the gain is read on the IF product. Each point is a harmonic-balance run of every element's mixer, about a second, so theta_in steps 5°. The NF is a harmonic-balance noise run from the wave's port, swept over theta_steer; its VAR block sets theta_in = theta_steer, so each of those runs is at its beam's peak. A phase shifter at the IF after an LO above the signal steers the inverted phase: its line is (k − 1)·(360° + dphi) long.

In sub-arrays the wave reaches every element, the phase step runs across the whole array, and the closed-form array factor weighs each element by its own amplitude to the output: its taper, its tree's parts and amplifiers, and its sub-array's path.

Levels at every node

The Levels tab and the Levels display follow the chain node by node: node 0 is the input and node k the output of stage k. At every node:

Quantity Budget
Signal Pin + G, per tone of two at the input power
Noise floor 10·log10(k·(Ts + Te)·B·Gn) + 30 dBm, the noise in the bandwidth
NF the cumulative noise figure
IM3 3·P − 2·OIP3, each third-order product of the two tones, absolute
Each blocker its input level plus every stage's gain at its own frequency: a filter's own response there (the model the Filter block simulates with, its IL included), an S-parameter data stage's file there, a mixer moving it to |f − Flo|
A canceller's interference from the canceller's input, where it is stated, and its residual after it
Margin to compression OP1dB − the larger of the signal and the blockers; before anything compresses, the whole chain's IP1dB less the input's
SNR the signal over the noise floor

The simulated points come from three benches: the Levels bench (two tones each at the input power: the signal and the IM3), the Blockers bench (the blockers alone, an isolator after every stage so that each node's voltage is the wave going forward, not a reflection standing on a filter's stopband) and the 1-Tone bench (each stage's cumulative NF, from the noise run's own shares, and the noise floor that NF gives at the node through the budget's noise gain). In the window they appear once those benches have been simulated beside the .cchain; in the display they are its points, the budget its lines. The displays plot against a variable nodeix that each bench sweeps around a trivial DC solve, which is how one number per node becomes one curve.

The dBm plots, in the window and in the display, reach 10 dB over the highest level they draw and 20 dB under the lowest level but the IM3, each rounded out to 10 dB, and half a node beyond the input and the output. Two tones far under the noise floor would otherwise take most of the height, so an IM3 under the frame is clipped there and its legend entry says so: IM3 (clipped). The dB plot reaches 10 dB beyond its NF, SNR and margin. A level that does not exist is left out, never drawn at a stand-in: the IM3 before anything is nonlinear, the interference before the canceller, and a blocker from the stage on that passes nothing of it (a band-pass filter at 0 Hz, where a mixer can put one).

The level diagram

Tick Levels in the Blocks view and the chain's level plan is drawn under its blocks, each node on the gap between two blocks: the input on the arrow before the first, each stage's output on the arrow after it.

At every node, in dBm:

Line What it is
signal Pin + G, its value written at each node
noise floor the noise in the bandwidth, kT·B with the cumulative NF and the gain, its value written at each node
sensitivity MDS + the required SNR, carried to the node by the gain: the signal the chain needs
P1dB the OP1dB of the stages up to the node, from the first stage that compresses, its value written at each node
IM3 each third-order product of two tones at the input power, from the first stage that has an intercept
each blocker, the interference as in the table above

Shaded between them: the SNR, from the noise floor up to the signal; the headroom, from the signal up to the P1dB; and, hatched, the SFDR, from the noise floor up to where the IM3 would reach it, (2/3)·(OIP3 − noise). The key under the plot gives the SNR and the SFDR at the output, and the margin to P1dB there as the Levels tab gives it: from the strongest carrier, which it names (the signal, or a blocker). Each line is named at the output with its last value. The figure is framed as the Levels tab is, and its window also holds the P1dB, the sensitivity and a link's EIRP; an IM3 under it is a ▼ on the bottom edge at its node, and its name at the output keeps its value. Over the plot, the frequency of each run of nodes, a dashed line at each mixer; in an array, the nodes that carry one element's levels are marked each of N elements: the branch the blocks draw once, "× N", up to the combiner.

A transmit chain's diagram is read toward its output. The signal is Pout, the output power at every node, and over the P1dB, dashed, is the Psat referred to each node: the ceiling the stages up to it give, P_k = min(P_(k−1) + g_k, Psat_k), the chain's Psat at the output. The shading under the P1dB is the back-off. The key gives the back-off at the output from both, the noise floor in dBm/Hz, and the ACLR estimated from the OIP3 (an estimate, as the relation says). There is no sensitivity and no SFDR, which are a receiver's.

With a link, its front stands left of the input: the EIRP, the path down to the power each element receives, the path's loss (and the receive antenna's gain) written on it, and the receiver's ceiling, IP1dB less RxBackoffDb, marked at the input. When the power arriving is above the ceiling it is drawn hollow, held down to it.

Click a node to select the stage whose output it is; the selected stage's node is drawn selected. Copy puts the blocks and the diagram on the clipboard together. circuitrf chain <file> --level-diagram levels.png (or .svg) draws the same diagram on its own, the nodes evenly spaced.

The canceller

A Canceller stage subtracts a weighted copy of an interference from the main path: a reference path from the interference's own source, through an amplitude setting, a phase setting and a delay, into a directional coupler's isolated port, the main path being the coupler's through arm.

Parameter Meaning
Coupling The coupler's coupling, dB. The main path loses 10·log10(1 − c) of it.
IL The coupler's excess loss, dB.
Pint The interference at the canceller's main input, dBm.
Bint The interference's bandwidth.
Pref The reference input: the interference at its source, dBm. The path's gain follows from it.
NFref The reference path's noise figure, dB. Blank: passive, at T0.
AmpErr, PhaseErr, DelayErr The cancellation path's amplitude error (dB), phase error (degrees, an advance) and delay mismatch (the reference path later, seconds: 0.1 ns).

On the wanted signal it is the through arm, a loss L_t = 10^(IL/10)/(1 − c), and the noise the reference path injects. That path needs a gain G_ref with G_ref·P_ref·c = P_int·(1 − c); its output is at T0·F_ref·G_ref, coupled by c/(1 − c) against the through arm, so

F = L_t + (F_ref·G_ref − 1)·c/(1 − c)

A passive path (F_ref·G_ref = 1) adds nothing to the coupler's loss.

On the interference the residual is the fraction R the subtraction leaves. With an amplitude ratio a = 10^(AmpErr/20), a phase error φ and a delay mismatch τ, a carrier of bandwidth B and flat spectrum, centred ν from where the phase was set, leaves the band's average of |1 − a·e^(j(φ − 2πfτ))|²:

R = 1 + a² − 2a·cos(φ − 2πντ)·sinc(πBτ),      sinc x = sin x / x,      depth = −10·log10 R

33.5 dB at 0.1 dB and 1°; with 1 ns of delay mismatch alone, 40.8 dB over 5 MHz, 28.8 dB over 20 MHz and 22.8 dB over 40 MHz. The window's Canceller tab draws the depth against the phase error for five amplitude errors, and against the bandwidth for four delay mismatches. The levels carry the interference and its residual node by node.

The Canceller bench studies it with real signals. Two MOD_Sources, which the Signal Designer edits: the wanted signal, an NR 64-QAM carrier and a QPSK one, and the interference, three NR carriers of 10, 5 and 20 MHz, the first two under the wanted ones. The interference is split: one share leaks into the main path through a line of 1 ns, the other is the reference path — an Amp for the amplitude, one path of a 2-way Combiner for a flat phase, a line for the delay — into the coupler's isolated port. Its VAR block sets the errors, amp_err, phase_err and delay_err, and two switches, canc_on (the reference path) and sig_on (the wanted signal). Its envelope runs:

  • the interference alone, uncancelled: the reference each depth is measured from;
  • the depth against each error, swept, the others at their nominal values, at every interference carrier: beside it the closed form above at that carrier's bandwidth and offset, so the 20 MHz carrier shows how a delay mismatch costs a wider signal more;
  • the wanted carriers with and without cancellation, their noise on: EVM, SNR, and each constellation both ways.

Open either source in the Signal Designer to change its modulation (LTE, NR, DBPSK, FSK, CSS and the rest it offers) or its bandwidth; the bench measures whatever it sends.

The modulated-signal demo

include a modulated-signal demo, in Transfer to Schematic's drop-down (or --demo, or "Demo": true in the .cchain), adds <chain> Demo: the chain demodulated end to end. Each element is fed an NR 64-QAM carrier and, from a second source beside it, a DBPSK carrier at twice the bandwidth's offset, joined by a 2-way Combiner, each at the input power and noisy at the source temperature. Each mixer's LO carries a phase-noise mask, which an envelope run plays as a random phase. An envelope run with Noise=yes and EvmSplit=yes is swept over the input power in seven steps, from 5 dB of SNR to 5 dB past the input P1dB. Its display:

  • the 64-QAM constellation at the output, received points over the ideal ones, at the middle and the highest power;
  • the EVM against the input power, 64-QAM and DBPSK, and beside it the budget's from its SNR, EVM ≈ 1/√SNR, which holds where noise dominates;
  • the EVM's split into its noise and distortion parts: noise at low power, the LO's phase noise as a floor, distortion past compression;
  • the SNR in the carrier's channel, simulated and the budget's.

A linear transmitter

The example's Linear TX.cchain is a 3.5 GHz transmitter for a 100 MHz NR carrier at 30 kHz subcarrier spacing, from a 200 MHz IF to the antenna:

Stage Part Gain NF Compression
IQ IQMod, LO 3.3 GHz at 7 dBm, upper sideband, 0.2 dB and 1.5° of imbalance, IsoLO_IF 50 dB −5.90 dB 12 dB IIP3 18.01 dBm (each mixer 15 dBm)
BPF1 Filter, 5th-order Butterworth, 3.4 to 3.6 GHz −1.5 dB 1.5 dB
DRV Amp 20 dB 4 dB OIP3 32 dBm (tanh)
PA Amp, Law = Rapp, Psat 37 dBm, P 2, Pdc 10 W 30 dB 6 dB IP1dB 5.84 dBm, cubic IIP3 15.47 dBm
BPF2 Filter, 5th-order 0.1 dB Chebyshev, 3.4 to 3.6 GHz −0.6 dB 0.6 dB

Driven at −14 dBm, its budget, every number of which an independent calculation reproduces to 10⁻⁶ dB from the formulas above (testdata/chain/tx_reference.py: the PA's 1 dB point and saturation by root-finding Rapp's own AM-AM, the tanh stages' compression by integrating the describing function); a test holds the budget to it at 10⁻⁶ dB:

Readout Value
Gain, NF 42.00 dB, 14.14 dB
Output power 28.00 dBm; as a CW carrier 27.95 dBm, 0.05 dB compressed
OP1dB, back-off 34.04 dBm, 6.04 dB
Psat, back-off 36.40 dBm, 8.40 dB
OIP3, ACLR 44.65 dBm, −38.07 dBc
Noise floor −117.84 dBm/Hz
Noise in a 20 MHz band 200 MHz above the carrier −156.50 dBm/Hz, −83.49 dBm: both filters' rejection, 30.7 and 34.4 dB there
Image, LO 35.17 dB rejected at the modulator, −167.82 dBc at the output; −23.22 dBc at the modulator, −90.27 dBc at the output

And its benches against it:

Quantity Budget Simulated Why it differs
Output over the drive, −34 to +4 dBm in the CW output 5×10⁻⁴ dB under at every drive the Chebyshev filter's 0.1 dB ripple at 3.5 GHz, which the budget leaves out
Output 18 dB past the operating point 36.3665 dBm 36.3659 dBm as above
IP1dB −6.96 dBm −6.86 dBm the cascaded-P1dB formula, as a receive chain's
Image, LO at the modulator −35.17, −23.22 dBc −35.17, −23.21 dBc
Image, LO at the output −167.82, −90.27 dBc −166.3, −90.36 dBc the image is the run's MaxMixOrder 5 truncation: at 9 it reads −167.88 dBc
Noise floor, 1 MHz off the carrier −117.84 dBm/Hz −117.98 dBm/Hz half the noise is amplitude, which the PA at its operating point passes 0.2245 dB under its gain, the other half its CW gain: 0.134 dB expected
Noise in the receive band −156.50 dBm/Hz −156.63 dBm/Hz as above
PA: AM-AM, AM-PM Rapp's law 6.5×10⁻¹⁰ dB, 10⁻¹⁵°
PA: IP1dB 5.835 dBm 5.826 dBm the bench's three-point interpolation
IM3 at the operating point −39.32 dBc −43.41 dBc the cubic with the PA's 1 dB point is pessimistic for P = 2 away from compression
ACLR at the operating point −38.07 dBc −39.07 dBc the estimate is optimistic at the PA (alone: −38.51 estimated, −37.73 and −37.86 simulated), and the band filter after it removes 1.43 dB of the regrowth, which the estimate does not have
Output, NR carrier 28.00 dBm 27.65 dBm the carrier's peaks, up to the PA's 1 dB point, compress
EVM, NR carrier — 4.09 % the PA's compression of the peaks

The PA alone, driven by the same NR carrier at its operating point (its own bench), puts out 28.38 dBm with −37.73 and −37.86 dBc of ACLR and 2.53 % EVM, at 6.88 % efficiency on its 10 W.

How closely the simulation agrees

Measured on the example's superhet and array, the budget against the simulation of the benches it writes:

Quantity Superhet 4-element array Why it differs at all
Gain −1.1×10⁻⁴ dB −1.1×10⁻⁴ dB The small-signal drive, 40 dB below IP1dB. An S-parameter bench reads 3×10⁻¹⁰ dB
NF, and each stage's +6.6×10⁻⁵ dB at most +1.0×10⁻⁴ dB at most The harmonic-balance noise run's 1 kHz offset from the IF, and its drive
IIP3 +1.8×10⁻⁴ dB +1.9×10⁻⁴ dB tanh's fifth-order term, 50 dB below the intercept
OIP3, and each stage's gain and OIP3 2.6×10⁻⁴ dB at most 2.6×10⁻⁴ dB at most as above
IP1dB +0.048 dB +0.062 dB The cascaded-P1dB formula is an approximation: the chain compresses a little later
SNR −0.13 dB −0.27 dB One noise record's statistics, about ±0.12 dB from seed to seed

The same array at RF, with no mixer, runs its noise through the S-parameter analysis instead and reads 3×10⁻¹⁰ dB in gain and 10⁻¹¹ dB in NF. The envelope SNR is a measurement of one noise record: four seeds of the array read 29.17 to 29.42 dB against 29.37 dB predicted.

The superhet's Levels bench puts the signal on the budget to 2×10⁻⁵ dB at every node and the IM3 to 8×10⁻⁵ dB; its Blockers bench reads each blocker 0.001 to 0.003 dB below the budget, the blocker's own slight compression at −40 and −50 dBm into the LNA. The front end's 1-Tone bench reads the canceller's noise, its through arm and the reference path's coupled noise, on the formula to 10⁻⁶ dB.

The Canceller bench's depth, at each of the three interference carriers and every swept error, is the closed form's to within 1.4 % of the depth, 0.7 dB at 49.7 dB deep and under 0.3 dB everywhere shallower than 45 dB. With cancellation the 64-QAM carrier's EVM falls from 840 % to 3.2 % and the QPSK one's from 1036 % to 8.6 %.

The superhet's Demo bench reads the SNR 0.20 dB under the budget at its lowest power, where noise dominates, and the EVM's noise part 57.0 % against the budget's 1/√SNR of 56.2 %. Higher up, two floors the budget does not model take over: the LO's phase noise, 1.23 % of EVM in the distortion part, which is the mask integrated over the channel (−38.2 dBc), and a noise part that stops at about 1 % (40 dB of SNR), which the Canceller bench's NR carriers show as well. At 5 dB past the input P1dB the distortion part is 15.5 %.

The dual-conversion receiver's benches, each conversion's against its own budget:

Quantity To IF1 From IF1 Why it differs at all
Gain −1.1×10⁻⁴ dB −1.1×10⁻⁴ dB the small-signal drive, as above
NF, and each stage's +3.1×10⁻⁵ dB +9.9×10⁻⁵ dB as above
IP1dB +0.033 dB +0.044 dB the cascaded-P1dB formula
Signal and IM3 at every node 1.1×10⁻⁵ and 2.5×10⁻⁵ dB 1.3×10⁻⁵ and 3.4×10⁻⁴ dB
Each blocker at every node 0.0013 to 0.0025 dB under 8×10⁻⁵ dB; the input +0.0018 dB the blockers' compression; the second conversion's input has no isolator in front of its roofing filter
SNR, envelope −0.45 dB +0.016 dB the first conversion ends at MIX1's output, 7.5 dB over a noise factor of 1.41, so the load's own noise, which the budget leaves out, is 1/7.9 of what reaches it: 0.52 dB

The two conversions' simulated gains added, and their noise factors cascaded by Friis, are the whole chain's budget to −2.2×10⁻⁴ dB and +8×10⁻⁵ dB. The whole chain's 2-Tone bench, four tones at MaxMixOrder 5, reads IIP3 and OIP3 3×10⁻³ dB high and every stage's OIP3 within 5×10⁻³ dB. Each conversion's Demo reads its SNR at the lowest power on its budget, once the load's noise is counted (−0.48 dB to MIX1's output, +0.08 dB to the end).

The 26 GHz link's receiver, run at the −59.41 dBm its link delivers to each element, reads −1.1×10⁻⁴ dB in gain and +2.8×10⁻⁴ dB in NF on its 1-Tone bench, +9×10⁻⁴ dB in IIP3 on its 2-Tone bench, and its eight-element Steering and Combiners benches 10⁻¹⁴ dB. Its Levels bench drives two tones each at that power, 24 dB under the receiver's input P1dB, and reads the mixer's output 0.013 dB under the budget, its IM3 0.030 dB: the tones' own slight compression. Its Envelope bench reads the SNR in the 50 MHz NR carrier's channel 0.02 dB under the budget's 43.15 dB. Its link has no circuit: EIRP, the path and every readout agree with an independent calculation (testdata/chain/link_reference.py) to 10⁻⁹ at five points. Its TX bench reads the output at 10 dB of overdrive 0.44 dB under Psat, and at the 8 dB back-off 0.92 dB under the budget's Psat − Backoff − Loss, at 6.3 % EVM and −30.3 dBc ACPR.

The array's Steering bench puts its pattern on the closed-form array factor to 3×10⁻⁹ dB within 3 dB of each peak and to 10⁻⁶ dB down to −60 dB, and its gain, NF and array gain at each peak on the budget to 10⁻¹⁴ dB. The Combiners bench reads each variant's gain and NF to 10⁻¹⁴ dB; each variant's intercepts and compression point, transferred on its own, read as the table above does.

Sub-arrays at RF, two of three, each an active tree with a pass-through and a taper: the 1-Tone bench reads gain and NF, and every stage's NF, exactly (an S-parameter run), the compression point 0.028 dB late, the 2-Tone bench IIP3 +1.7×10⁻⁴ dB and OIP3 −8.7×10⁻⁵ dB, and the Steering bench the pattern on the array factor of every element's own amplitude and the gain, NF and array gain at each peak to 10⁻¹⁴ dB. Through a mixer, six elements on one LO: the Steering bench reads the gain at each peak 2.8×10⁻⁴ dB low (the wave's own slight compression, 40 dB under the array's), the NF and array gain within 1.1×10⁻⁴ dB, and the pattern on the array factor to 2.8×10⁻⁴ dB within 40 dB of the peak, with the LO below the signal or above it; the Combiners bench each variant's gain within 2.2×10⁻⁴ dB and NF within 1.2×10⁻⁴ dB. The budget of each combiner is an independent calculation's (testdata/chain/arrays_reference.py, which sums the network source by source) to 10⁻⁹ dB.

The linear transmitter's benches are tabled with it, in A linear transmitter: its output over 38 dB of drive on the budget's CW output to 5×10⁻⁴ dB, its PA's AM-AM and AM-PM on Rapp's law to 10⁻⁹, its modulator's image and LO on their closed forms, its noise 0.13 to 0.15 dB under the budget (0.134 dB expected), its two-tone IM3 4.1 dB under the estimate, and its ACLR 0.8 dB over the estimate at the PA and 1.0 dB under it at the output, where the band filter takes 1.43 dB of the regrowth.

The .cchain file

A .cchain is JSON. The system inputs are numbers whose names carry their unit; a stage's parameters are text, exactly as the part's netlist line carries them.

{
  "FormatVersion": 1,
  "FrequencyHz": 2450000000,
  "BandwidthHz": 4500000,
  "InputPowerDbm": -70,
  "TemperatureK": 290,
  "RequiredSnrDb": 10,
  "Stages": [
    { "Name": "LNA", "Part": "Amp", "Parameters": { "Gain": "16", "NF": "1", "IP3": "15", "IP3Ref": "Output" } },
    { "Name": "RFBPF", "Part": "Filter", "Parameters": { "Response": "Butterworth", "F1": "2.35 GHz", "F2": "2.55 GHz", "IL": "1.5" } },
    { "Name": "MIX", "Part": "Mixer", "Parameters": { "ConvGain": "-7", "NF": "7", "IIP3": "10", "Plo": "7", "Flo": "2.1 GHz" } }
  ]
}
Key Meaning
FormatVersion 1; 2 for a chain that uses a value of the frequency, a budget-only parameter, a Levels combiner, a link, a sweep or a readout input; 3 for a transmit chain, an IQ modulator, an Amplifier's Law, Psat, P, PhiSat or PhiMax, or a converter's Sideband; 4 for sub-arrays (a second Combiner), a tree's Ways or one whose N is not a power of 2, or PathIL on an active combiner. A file from a newer circuitRF is refused, not read in part.
Direction Optional: "Transmit" for a transmit chain. Absent: a receive chain.
RxBandOffsetHz, RxBandHz Optional: a transmit chain's receive band, its centre's offset from the carrier at the output and its width.
FrequencyHz, BandwidthHz, InputPowerDbm, TemperatureK, RequiredSnrDb The system inputs. Absent: 2.45 GHz, 1 MHz, −70 dBm, 290 K, 10 dB.
Stages In signal order. Name follows the instance-name rule (a letter, then letters, digits and _).
Part Amp, Mixer, IQMod, Atten, Filter, Switch, Circulator, Coupler, PhaseShifter, Limiter, Canceller, Splitter, SnP or Combiner.
Parameters The part's parameters by their own names. An absent one takes the part's default (a System block's own placement default); one the part does not list is carried onto the schematic unchanged and not read by the budget.
Blockers Optional: [{"OffsetHz": 150000000, "LevelDbm": -40}, …], each an offset from FrequencyHz and a level at the input.
Demo Optional: true to write the demo bench too.
FractionalBandwidth, Streams, NfAllowanceDb, RxBackoffDb Optional: the readouts' inputs. Absent: the stated bandwidth, 1, 1 dB, 10 dB.
Link Optional: {"Tx": {"Psat": "…", …}, "Path": {"Distance": "200 m", …}}, the link's inputs by name, as a stage's parameters are.
Sweeps Optional: [{"Of": "Frequency", "From": 20e9, "To": 40e9, "Points": 41}, …], Of one of Frequency, TxElements, RxElements. See Sweeps.

A second Combiner makes sub-arrays. An SnP stage's File is a path; a relative one resolves from the workspace the .cchain belongs to, or its own folder when it belongs to none, and so does a table's.

From the command line

circuitrf chain Superhet.cchain                      the cascade, as the window shows it
circuitrf chain Superhet.cchain -o budget.npy        the budget as a DataSet: per-stage cubes over a stage axis
circuitrf chain "26 GHz Link.cchain" -o link.npy     the link's numbers as scalars, each sweep a group of its own
circuitrf chain Superhet.cchain --level-diagram levels.svg   the level diagram, as a .svg or a .png
circuitrf chain Superhet.cchain --to-schematic       the benches and their displays, beside the .cchain
circuitrf hb "Superhet 2-Tone/schematic/Superhet 2-Tone.csch"

A transmit chain's report reads its output in place of a receiver's sensitivity: the output power and its CW compression, the back-off from OP1dB and from Psat, the ACLR, the noise floor and the receive band's noise, and an IQ modulator's image and LO.

--to-schematic [dir] writes into another folder, --name names the benches, --demo adds the demo bench, and an existing bench is a refusal unless --replace is given. circuitrf check reads a .cchain through the same budget and reports its refusals. Over the MCP server the verb is run analysis=chain.
